quotes: "These nuances underscore a pressing need for preference-driven captioning approaches that allow viewers to adapt captions to their personal goals and preferences—whether clarity, immersion, or efficiency—and align them with the tone and style of the media." (p. 2)

entries.value: creators would otherwise need to author the possible caption variations themselves. (PDF p. 6)
quotes: "Rather than authoring all possible variations, creators define a two-dimensional space—bounded by parameters of Level of Detail and Expressiveness—within which AI-transformations can occur." (p. 6)

entries.value: creators set example bounds, inspect generated previews, and edit or lock exceptions while AI produces variations. (PDF p. 7)
quotes: "Together, these mechanisms allow creators to maintain fine-grained editorial control while leveraging the efficiency of AI assistance." (p. 7)

entries.value: M2, M3, M4, M9 — the anchor, preview, override, and rewrite supports jointly produce this workflow shift.
author_claim — the paper explicitly contrasts authoring every variation with defining a bounded transformation space.
author_assertion — the prior process is stated by the authors rather than measured in a comparison condition.
viewers received a single fixed caption track that could not reflect diverse preferences. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "However, conventional NSI captioning systems face a fundamental limitation: they adopt a 'one-size-fits-all' approach, where creators provide a single, fixed caption track that may fail to account for the diversity in viewers’ backgrounds and preferences." (p. 2)

entries.value: viewers select bounded style coordinates, representation and genre options, or conversationally stated preferences while the video plays. (PDF p. 8)
quotes: "Viewers can specify their preferences through direct manipulation or natural language interactions. Transformations occur seamlessly during video playback." (p. 8)

entries.value: M5, M6, M7, M8, M9 — the viewer controls and resulting adaptive caption jointly produce this shift.
author_claim — the paper describes real-time viewer customization but does not compare it experimentally with fixed captions.
author_assertion — the fixed-track baseline is an introductory account of conventional practice.

rq3_entries.value: the system detects and highlights non-speech items, extracts audio-visual context, interprets viewer preferences, maps them relative to creator anchors, recalibrates linked parameters, and generates caption wording. (PDF pp. 6, 9)
quotes: "The system automatically detects non-speech caption—e.g., those enclosed in brackets or parentheses—and visually highlights them with yellow borders." (p. 6)

"The Node.js server handled decoding caption files, parsing user preferences, and communicating with the GPT-4o model (via the OpenAI API) for caption transformations and natural language interpretations." (p. 9)

rq3_entries.value: creators decide acceptable bounds, judge previews, and edit or lock wording; viewers choose or state preferences and retain interpretive judgment over the captions. (PDF pp. 7–8)
quotes: "Sam defines the transformation space by setting two anchor points that represent the acceptable range for viewer customization." (p. 7)
"Viewers can specify their preferences through direct manipulation or natural language interactions." (p. 8)

rq3_entries.value: no — neither evaluation measured learning or skill development.
not_measured — no learning direction was tested.
author_raised — the paper reports concern that AI wording could displace viewers’ own interpretation. (PDF p. 12)
quotes: "Many participants expressed concerns that AI-generated captions might be overly interpretive, potentially undermining their ability to form an independent understanding of the content." (p. 12)

rq3_entries.value: no — controls remain available during playback; any simplification is selected by the viewer rather than withdrawn as competence grows. (PDF p. 8)
quotes: "Transformations occur seamlessly during video playback." (p. 8)

rq3_entries.value: creators must continue defining acceptable ranges and resolving wording, while viewers must continue selecting or articulating preferences; the paper reports no competence-linked change in those responsibilities. (PDF pp. 7–8)
quotes: "If a generated transformation is close but not quite right, Sam can manually edit it to achieve the desired result." (p. 7)
"Viewers can specify their preferences through direct manipulation or natural language interactions." (p. 8)

rq3_entries.value: single_session (1 per participant) — the viewer evaluation was one approximately 90-minute remote session; the creator evaluation was likewise a single approximately 60-minute session. (PDF pp. 9, 11)
quotes: "All sessions were conducted remotely via Zoom and lasted approximately 60 minutes." (p. 9)
"The IRB-approved study lasted approximately 90 minutes and was conducted remotely via Zoom." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: the evaluations enhanced DHH viewers’ narrative engagement while preserving creators’ creative intent. (PDF p. 15)
quotes: "Our evaluations showed that the system enhanced narrative engagement for DHH viewers while preserving creators’ creative intent." (p. 15)

claim_entries.value: preference — the claim concerns experienced engagement and perceived preservation of intent, not objective performance or learning. (PDF p. 15)
quotes: "Our evaluations showed that the system enhanced narrative engagement for DHH viewers while preserving creators’ creative intent." (p. 15)

claim_entries.value: empirical — the strongest claim is based on studies with caption creators and DHH viewers. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "We evaluated CapTune through user studies with seven creators and twelve DHH participants, assessing usability, support for narrative engagement, and perceived quality of the adapted captions." (p. 2)

claim_entries.value: single_condition_usability — both participant groups explored CapTune and discussed it without a control system or randomized condition. (PDF p. 11)
quotes: "The core of the session involved hands-on exploration with the system." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: 19 — seven caption creators and twelve DHH viewers participated in the evaluations. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "We evaluated CapTune through user studies with seven creators and twelve DHH participants, assessing usability, support for narrative engagement, and perceived quality of the adapted captions." (p. 2)

claim_entries.value: mixed — the sample combines experienced video/caption creators with DHH caption viewers. (PDF pp. 9–10)
quotes: "We evaluated the Creator Tool with participants who have experience creating and editing videos and captions." (p. 9)
"We recruited 12 DHH participants (seven female, five male; aged 23–67, M=38.3, SD=16.7) who regularly use closed captions when consuming video content." (p. 10)

claim_entries.value: none — neither evaluation included a control condition, baseline system, or ablation.
descriptive_only — the paper reports counts, demographics, and coding reliability but no inferential outcome test. (PDF p. 11)
quotes: "Interrater reliability (IRR) measured using Cohen’s Kappa [51] was, on average, 0.74, and the raw agreement was 90.5%." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: creator sessions lasted approximately 60 minutes and viewer sessions approximately 90 minutes. (PDF pp. 9, 11)
quotes: "All sessions were conducted remotely via Zoom and lasted approximately 60 minutes." (p. 9)
"The IRB-approved study lasted approximately 90 minutes and was conducted remotely via Zoom." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: only three viewers used chat, seven found tuning trial-and-error, and six found the style grid overly dense or difficult to navigate. (PDF p. 11)
quotes: "However, only three participants used the chat interface, suggesting that while it was appreciated as a supplementary feature, most viewers gravitated toward the direct visual controls." (p. 11)
"Seven participants found the process of tuning parameters to be a matter of trial-and-error that 'took the attention away from the video itself' (P5)." (p. 11)
"Six participants found the 10 × 10 style grid overly dense or difficult to navigate." (p. 11)

claim_entries.value: claim_exceeds_evidence — single-session qualitative reports support perceived engagement and control, but not an unqualified causal enhancement or verified semantic preservation. (PDF p. 14)
quotes: "While these insights offer depth and a user-centered perspective, they do not provide systematic metrics of caption transformation accuracy or consistency." (p. 14)

claim_entries.value: the claim that the system enhanced engagement and preserved intent is stronger than uncontrolled self-report and qualitative feedback can establish, especially without accuracy or consistency metrics. (PDF pp. 14–15)
quotes: "Finally, our evaluation methodology focused on qualitative feedback from creators and DHH participants." (p. 14)
"Our evaluations showed that the system enhanced narrative engagement for DHH viewers while preserving creators’ creative intent." (p. 15)

paper_code_entries.value: accessible non-speech-caption authoring and personalized video viewing — the work spans creator-side caption production and DHH viewers’ use of adapted captions. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "We introduce CapTune, a system for personalized transformation of NSI captions using creator-defined constraints and viewer-controlled parameters." (p. 2)

paper_code_entries.value: immediate_performance_or_sensemaking — the implemented support adapts captions for viewers’ current preferences, needs, and viewing contexts; educational use is only envisioned. (PDF p. 13)
quotes: "Using this tool, DHH viewers can adapt non-speech captions to better suit their preferences, needs, and viewing contexts." (p. 13)

paper_code_entries.value: unspecified — the paper recruits experienced creators and caption-using DHH viewers but does not frame either population by a novice-to-expert progression.
knowledge_or_concept_gap — inaccessible auditory cues can leave DHH viewers without information about what a sound is like. (PDF p. 13)
quotes: "I would have never known what it sounded like if this description had not come up." (p. 13)

paper_code_entries.value: process — the evaluations assess usability and interaction with the creator and viewer workflows. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "We evaluated CapTune through user studies with seven creators and twelve DHH participants, assessing usability, support for narrative engagement, and perceived quality of the adapted captions." (p. 2)

paper_code_entries.value: artifact — participants assessed perceived quality and meaning of the adapted caption outputs. (PDF p. 2)
quotes: "We evaluated CapTune through user studies with seven creators and twelve DHH participants, assessing usability, support for narrative engagement, and perceived quality of the adapted captions." (p. 2)

paper_code_entries.value: structuring — the tool organizes acceptable caption variation into explicit axes and creator-set bounds. (PDF p. 6)
quotes: "Rather than authoring all possible variations, creators define a two-dimensional space—bounded by parameters of Level of Detail and Expressiveness—within which AI-transformations can occur." (p. 6)

paper_code_entries.value: contingency — the displayed caption responds to the viewer’s selected grid cell during interaction. (PDF p. 8)
quotes: "By selecting the cell (Level of Detail = 6, Expressiveness = 5), Jamie transforms [Loud thunder sound] to [Rumbling thunder crashes violently]." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: adaptation — captions are transformed during playback from current viewer preferences. (PDF p. 8)
quotes: "Transformations occur seamlessly during video playback." (p. 8)

paper_code_entries.value: distributed_support — creators define constraints, AI transforms, and viewers choose, making the support jointly produced across people and tool. (PDF p. 13)
quotes: "CapTune reframes non-speech captions as dynamic, co-authored experiences—constructed not solely by creators or viewers, but collaboratively negotiated through constrained AI transformations." (p. 13)

paper_code_entries.value: hybrid_or_multi_model — GPT-4o transforms and interprets preferences, while VideoLLaMA2 supplies audio-visual scene descriptions. (PDF pp. 6, 9)
quotes: "VideoLLaMA2 outputs detailed textual descriptions of each segment’s visual and audio content, providing essential context for accurate caption transformations." (p. 6)

"The Node.js server handled decoding caption files, parsing user preferences, and communicating with the GPT-4o model (via the OpenAI API) for caption transformations and natural language interpretations." (p. 9)

paper_code_entries.value: llm_era — large language and video-language models generate the semantic content and transformations. (PDF p. 5)
quotes: "Rather than relying on predefined rules or static templates, CapTune leverages large language models guided by creators’ specifications and viewer preferences to dynamically adapt captions, preserving narrative coherence and creative intent while addressing diverse accessibility needs." (p. 5)

limitations: "First, the four customization parameters in CapTune—though grounded in our findings—represent a simplification of the rich, fluid space of DHH preferences." (p. 14)
"A linear interpolation model may not fully capture shifting needs across scenes, genres, or emotional contexts." (p. 14)
"Second, our evaluation focused on short-form content, with clips ranging from 2 to 8 minutes in length." (p. 14)

"Longer content, such as full-length films or episodic television, introduces additional challenges related to narrative consistency, viewer fatigue, and cumulative comprehension—factors that our current study does not yet address." (p. 14)
"Third, the system relies on the GPT-4o model, which, despite the guardrails we implemented, can still produce inconsistent or semantically inaccurate outputs." (p. 14)
"Finally, our evaluation methodology focused on qualitative feedback from creators and DHH participants." (p. 14)
"While these insights offer depth and a user-centered perspective, they do not provide systematic metrics of caption transformation accuracy or consistency." (p. 14)
boundary_conditions: "We evaluated the Creator Tool with participants who have experience creating and editing videos and captions." (p. 9)
"We recruited 12 DHH participants (seven female, five male; aged 23–67, M=38.3, SD=16.7) who regularly use closed captions when consuming video content." (p. 10)
"Second, our evaluation focused on short-form content, with clips ranging from 2 to 8 minutes in length." (p. 14)
cards.notes: - The core capability barrier is inaccessible auditory information rather than missing conceptual knowledge. `capability_gap` has no perceptual-access value; coded `knowledge_or_concept_gap`, which loses that sensory-access distinction.
cards.work_domain: accessible non-speech-caption authoring and personalized video viewing
cards.claim: the evaluations enhanced DHH viewers’ narrative engagement while preserving creators’ creative intent
